subject: Forensic Medicine
title: Firearm Wounds & Mechanical Injuries
preview: In forensic medicine, wound interpretation requires morphology, scene evidence and medical correlation rather than a single absolute sign.

sections.title: Incised wound versus laceration
points: Sharp-force incisions often have relatively clean margins, whereas blunt-force lacerations can show crushing and bridges of tissue.
Context can complicate appearance, especially over bony prominences.

sections.title: Interpret firearm injuries cautiously
points: Consider abrasion collars, soot, stippling, range, trajectory and secondary impacts only as a pattern of evidence.
A suspected entry or exit wound cannot be assigned accurately from a single surface feature in all cases.

sections.title: Exam trap
points: Do not declare a definitive range or manner of injury from one isolated sign.
A thorough medico-legal examination requires documentation and appropriate chain of custody.

quickRevision: An incised wound usually has sharply defined edges and little tissue bridging.
Lacerations from blunt force often have irregular margins and tissue bridges, although overlap occurs.
Entry/exit interpretation in firearm injury requires scene, trajectory, range and weapon information.

quiz.question: What is needed to interpret firearm injury findings?
options: Scene, trajectory, wound morphology and forensic correlation
quiz.explanation: Scene, trajectory, wound morphology and forensic correlation. Incised Wound vs Lacerated Wound Differentiation: • Incised Wound: Sharp weapon; length > depth; clean-cut regular margins; no tissue bridging; hair cut sharply; no bruising of surrounding skin.
